newsitem.title: NORWAY: Israel keeps making new conditions - Arafat in Oslo.
newsitem.headline: Israel keeps making new conditions - Arafat in Oslo.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat accused Israel on Monday of inconsistency in peace talks and insisted he was committed to solving deadlocked negotiations.
Arafat arrived in the Norwegian capital from a failed all-night bid to agree on a partial Israeli withdrawal from the occupied West Bank city of Hebron.
His visit marked a return to the cradle of hopes for peace -- Norway's government, which invited him, played a key role in a 1993 pact on Palestinian self-rule.

"I am sorry to say that still the Israelis are making new conditions every day, every day new conditions," said Arafat, back in the city where he shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize for the historic Israeli-PLO pact.
Arafat spoke to reporters after meeting new Norwegian Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland, who replaced Gro Harlem Brundtland last Friday.
Arafat said he asked Norway to help revive the flagging peace process.
He dismissed Israeli charges he was stalling after negotiators failed to agree on the pullout.
"I am completely committed to the peace process," he said. "You have to remember that all the Arab leaders...are committed to the peace process."

Arafat said he was travelling to Europe to get "another push from outside" for peace as U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross said he was leaving Israel, having failed in another effort to wrap up a deal.
But Arafat on Monday said Ross, who had warned the trip to Europe might hamper mediation efforts, would be back.
"I am sorry to say until six o'clock this morning we did not arrive at a final conclusion ... but he will return and we agreed that all the subcommittees will continue," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton on Sunday urged both Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in separate telephone calls to seal a deal.
Arafat said he believed it was possible to achieve agreement on Hebron before the U.S. elections on November 5.
"He (Clinton) is continuing his effort to achieve something concrete in the peace proces in the Middle East especially between Palestinians and the Israelis," Arafat said.
Palestinians have said Israel is trying to renegotiate terms of the Hebron withdrawal which the Jewish state agreed to more than a year ago.

Palestinians have said their remaining differences centre on Israel's demand for a right to pursue Palestinian militants into parts of Hebron it hands over to the PLO and on what arms Palestinian police would be allowed to carry.

Netanyahu has insisted on modifying security arrangements set in a redeployment deal which Israel's previous Labour-led government signed with the PLO. About 400 Jewish settlers live in enclaves in Hebron among 100,000 Palestinians.
The troop redeployment has been delayed since March.
Arafat shared the Peace Prize with then-Israeli foreign minister Shimon Peres and late prime minister Yitzhak Rabin for the now-troubled agreement on Palestinian self-rule.

On Tuesday, he was due to be received by King Harald V before holding final talks with Godal and leaving for Dublin, where the Palestinian leader will meet Ireland's prime minister, foreign minister and president during a two-day visit.
